title: Shiloh, the Survey, and Benjamin's Lot
summary: Israel gathers at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting there. Seven tribes still have no inheritance, and Joshua rebukes their delay, sends out three men from each to survey and write down the land in seven portions, and casts lots for them before the LORD. The first lot falls to Benjamin, whose borders and cities, lying between Judah and Joseph, are then described.
story: Judah and Joseph have received their land, but the other seven tribes are hanging back. The move to Shiloh marks a new stage: the tabernacle, which had traveled with Israel since Sinai, now stands in the middle of the land, and the rest of the allotments are made "in the presence of the LORD" there. Joshua's question in verse 3 shows that the problem is not the enemy but Israel's own slowness to take up what God has given. The chapter begins the allotment of the remaining tribes, which continues through chapter 19, with Benjamin first. Benjamin's small strip of land between the two great tribes will matter far beyond its size, for it contains Jerusalem, Gibeon, Bethel, and Gibeah.
historical:
Shiloh, identified with Khirbet Seilun in the hills of Ephraim north of Bethel, became Israel's central sanctuary for the period of the judges. There Hannah prayed for a son and Samuel grew up under the priest Eli (1 Samuel 1-3). After the ark was captured by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4), Shiloh fades from the story, and the prophets later pointed to its ruin as a warning (Jeremiah 7:12; Psalm 78:60). Excavations at the site in the twentieth century, including work by Danish teams and by Israel Finkelstein in the 1980s, have found remains from the early Iron Age, and many archaeologists connect a destruction there with the Philistine wars, though the details are debated.

Benjamin's towns include many that became famous. Jerusalem (Jebus) lay on the border with Judah and is listed here among Benjamin's cities, though neither tribe held it until David. Gibeah was Saul's hometown; Ramah was Samuel's; Mizpah was a gathering place for Israel in Samuel's time; Bethel and Gibeon had their own long histories. Israel's first king, Saul, came from Benjamin, and so, centuries later, did the apostle Paul (Philippians 3:5).
cultural:
Joshua's survey (verses 4-9) is a rare Old Testament scene of men sent out to map land for distribution. The men went "city by city" and returned with a written document (verse 9), a record of settlements and territories that could then be divided fairly. Writing in this period was a specialized skill, but written administrative lists were common across the ancient Near East.

Casting lots before the LORD placed the final decision outside human control. The exact method is not described; it may have involved marked stones or similar objects drawn or thrown. Proverbs 16:33 expresses the conviction behind the practice: though the lot is cast into the lap, its every decision is from the LORD. Doing this at the tabernacle, with the priest present (19:51), made the allotment an act of worship and a public, binding decision that no tribe could later dispute.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-10 are narrative, built around Joshua's rebuke and instructions, and they repeat key phrases: survey, map, return, cast lots, and in the presence of the LORD. Verse 1 opens with a significant sentence: the land "was subdued before them." Verses 11-28 are a boundary description and town list for Benjamin in the style of chapters 15-17. The north border (verses 12-13) follows the line described as Ephraim's southern border in chapter 16, and the south border (verses 15-19) retraces Judah's northern border from chapter 15 in reverse, so the careful reader sees how the tribal lands fit together like pieces of a map.

outline.t: The Tent of Meeting at Shiloh; seven tribes waiting
Joshua rebukes the delay and orders a survey
The survey and the lots at Shiloh

doctrines.note: The land is distributed by lot before the LORD, so that each tribe's portion is received as God's decision. His rule extends to what looks like chance.
The Tent of Meeting stands at the center of the land, and the whole congregation gathers there. Israel's life as a people is organized around God's presence among them in worship.

Joshua's question, "How long will you put off entering and possessing the land" (verse 3), exposes a failure to take up what God has already given. Faith is not only believing a promise but acting on it.

words.note: Kavash, to subdue. The same verb appears in Genesis 1:28, where humanity is told to fill the earth and subdue it. Its use in verse 1, as the land is subdued and the sanctuary set up, suggests that Israel's settlement in the land echoes the first calling given to humanity.

Raphah, to sink, relax, or be slack. Joshua asks how long the tribes will be slack about entering the land. The word describes a loss of energy or will, not open rebellion, which makes it a searching diagnosis.

Goral, lot, and by extension the portion decided by lot. The word appears five times here. Psalm 16:5 uses it when the psalmist says that the LORD holds his lot, taking the image of a family's allotted land and applying it to God's care for a person's whole life.
Katav, to write. The surveyors were to write a description of the land. The written record made the division public and permanent and shows administration by document, not by rumor or force.

christ: The chapter's central image is God's dwelling set up in the middle of the land, with his people gathered around it to receive their inheritance. The tabernacle at Shiloh foreshadows the temple, and the New Testament says that in Jesus the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us (John 1:14, where the Greek word means to pitch a tent). Paul also speaks of believers receiving an inheritance in Christ, assigned by God's purpose (Ephesians 1:11). The survey and the lots show inheritance received as gift; the Christian hope is framed the same way, as an inheritance given by God rather than seized.
questions: Joshua asked the tribes how long they would put off possessing what God had given them. What have you been slow to take up, even though God has already put it within reach?
The land was divided in the presence of the LORD. How might it change your decisions to make them consciously before God?
Benjamin's small territory held towns that shaped Israel's history. What small place or role in your life might matter more than its size suggests?
